claims.text: CVE-2025-6514 (CVSS 9.6, JFrog, July 2025) affected mcp-remote 0.0.5-0.1.15: a malicious or man-in-the-middle remote MCP server could return a crafted OAuth authorization_endpoint URL that caused local OS command execution when the proxy opened the browser.
The official GitHub MCP server exposes over 90 tools consuming 46k+ tokens, including high-risk operations like delete_file and delete_workflow_run_logs alongside benign tools like get_pull_requests.
Without a gateway, the practical MCP tool limit is 20 to 50 tools under context pressure; the mcp-gateway project claims tools are discoverable on demand instead.
The mcp-gateway project presents the agent with a compact meta-surface of 9 to 17 tools instead of every backend tool definition, while fronting MCP servers and REST APIs.

The mcp-gateway project provides bearer tokens, API keys, admin keys, per-client rate limits, opt-in circuit breakers, and a security firewall with credential redaction, prompt-injection detection, and shell/SQL/path-traversal scanning.

The MCPTox benchmark (August 2025) tested 20 LLM agents across 45+ real-world MCP servers with 353 tools; o1-mini had a 72.8% attack success rate, and Claude 3.7 Sonnet had the highest refusal rate but still under 3%.
More capable models are often more susceptible to tool poisoning because the attacks exploit superior instruction-following.
Between January and February 2026, 30+ CVEs were filed targeting MCP infrastructure, 43% of them exec/shell injection.
CVE-2025-53773 (CVSS 7.8): prompt injection in source files manipulates GitHub Copilot into enabling 'YOLO mode' (auto-approve all tools), achieving full RCE including MCP server injection.

Check Point Research showed (CVE-2025-59536, CVSS 8.7; CVE-2026-21852, CVSS 5.3) that malicious .mcp.json files in untrusted repositories could run arbitrary shell commands on tool initialization and exfiltrate Anthropic API keys before any user trust decision.

CVE-2026-32211 (CVSS 9.1, disclosed April 3, 2026): the @azure-devops/mcp server lacked authentication on its local listener, letting any process or browser-reachable origin enumerate Azure DevOps data via MCP tool calls.

The SANDWORM_MODE npm worm (Socket, February 20, 2026) planted a rogue MCP server under ~/.dev-utils/ via an McpInject module, registering innocuous-sounding tools whose descriptions carried prompt injection to steal SSH keys, AWS credentials, npm tokens and .env files, spread via 19 typosquatted packages.

The OWASP AISVS MCP chapter describes the MCP auth requirements as OAuth 2.1 + PKCE (S256) mandatory, RFC 8707 Resource Indicators required, step-up authorization, and token passthrough explicitly forbidden.

Incidents such as a Square OAuth bypass, the Azure DevOps MCP missing-auth CVE, and CVE-2026-52870 (Python SDK Tasks missing per-session authorization, fixed in 1.27.2) show that authentication and transport isolation do not replace tool-, argument-, and object-level authorization.
Solo.io agentgateway and Cloudflare Access with MCP Server Portals add gateway-level OAuth 2.1 enforcement, RBAC, and DLP; AWS IAM context keys (April 2026) distinguish agent from human callers.
In September 2025, researchers found the first known malicious MCP server in the wild: a compromised npm package called postmark-mcp.

In November 2025, a WhatsApp MCP integration was exploited via a malicious MCP server that poisoned tool descriptions with hidden instructions, silently redirecting message data to an attacker-controlled phone number.

In November 2025, Anthropic's official Git MCP server was found to have critical vulnerabilities (path validation bypass, argument injection, unsafe repository initialization) that could be chained with a filesystem MCP server for remote code execution via prompt injection.

In a widely cited 2025 demonstration, a GitHub issue planted in a public repository caused an agent using the GitHub MCP server to read the user's private repository data and publish it in a pull request.
MCP relies on OAuth 2.1 bearer tokens without specifying protocol-level token lifecycle management (refresh, revocation, reuse control), which can enable replay or session hijacking.

Some MCP orchestrators auto-resolve tool names from public registries or local modules, and clients often cannot specify unique tool identifiers or strict resolution policies, enabling tool name collisions that hijack execution.

Enterprises are converging on internal MCP registries/catalogs of vetted, approved servers as the governance unit, combined with strict authorization scoping, allowlisting, and treating every tool response as untrusted input.

Tool poisoning exploits a trust gap between connect-time review of a tool's description and runtime, when a server can return malicious instructions in live responses; mitigations include fixed-schema tool outputs and isolating high-privilege tools from external servers.

The MCP spec of 2026-07-28 made RFC 9728 protected-resource metadata and audience validation mandatory and left per-tool scopes to servers; agentgateway 1.6.0 evaluates CEL authorization on mcp.tool.arguments and hides denied items from lists.

The MCP Registry remains in 'preview', with server.json metadata under verified namespaces but no tool-level or security metadata; A2A 1.0 is stable but only Atlassian's Rovo connector among the surveyed tools consumes it.
